description: We are a team of passionate and innovative students driven by curiosity, creativity, and a shared ambition to turn space technology into meaningful solutions for Earth. . By combining technology, geospatial analysis, and collaborative problem-solving, we strive to transform complex Earth-observation data into accessible insights. We believe in learning by building, challenging conventional approaches, and creating solutions that can make a real-world impact.
summary:
SARVision: See What the Earth Hides is an independent student web app built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 (“Dancing with the SARs”). It turns synthetic aperture radar (SAR) observations into plain-language insight about a changing Earth. It is designed around NISAR, the joint NASA-ISRO radar mission, but currently runs on clearly labelled simulated data: 7 study areas and 168 scenes.

The web app has eight sections:

Overview: headline stats, recent changes and mission background.
Explore Earth: a map of the study areas.
Change Detection: compares two observation dates using a dB log-ratio and an adjustable threshold, then reports a change mask and statistics.
Flood Intelligence: maps potential new water and tracks water cover over time.
Vegetation Watch: follows canopy backscatter in forest regions.
Time Explorer: plays back every observation date for one region.
SAR Learning Lab: explains how radar works, compares radar with optical imaging and includes a glossary.
Data & Methodology: lists data sources and an eight-step processing method.

Its defining principle is honesty. Results are always called “potential” change, since soil moisture, season or speckle can mimic real events. It states that it is not an emergency warning system, and the planned link to real NISAR data (via ASF, Earthdata) is still to come.
details:
What it does and how it works

SARVision is a web app that makes radar satellite data understandable to non-experts. A person picks a study area and two observation dates. The app computes the difference in radar backscatter in decibels (a log-ratio), applies an adjustable threshold of 2 to 6 dB, and produces a change mask with statistics: percent of scene changed, affected area in km² and mean change. Dedicated modules cover flood mapping (smooth water looks dark to radar, so cells below -17.5 dB are classed as potential water), forest backscatter tracking, and a time slider that plays back every observation. A learning lab explains SAR, and a methodology page traces every number to a data source and processing step.

Benefits

  • It makes radar imagery readable without a remote-sensing background.
  • It shows how radar sees through cloud and darkness, where optical imagery can’t.
  • It is transparent: every result is traceable, and all findings are labelled “potential.”

Intended impact

The project aims to prepare students, educators and early-stage analysts for NISAR, the joint NASA-ISRO mission that will observe all land and ice every 12 days. It builds radar literacy and shows how open data can support flood, vegetation and land-change awareness once the real data layer is connected.

Tools and technologies

The recording shows a Leaflet map with Esri World Imagery and OpenStreetMap basemaps, a React-style single-page web interface and a hosted preview deployment. The planned data sources are NISAR products via ASF, NASA Earthdata and with Sentinel-1 as a reference. No special hardware is required. Please add anything I can’t see, such as the backend language, analysis libraries or AI tools. In my own recreation I used plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with SVG charts and a canvas-based radar simulation.

Creativity

  • Honesty is the central design choice. Simulated data is labelled everywhere, caveats sit next to results, and the app says it is not an emergency warning system.
  • Radar is taught through interaction: you run the analysis yourself and see the mask appear.
  • The project is “NISAR-ready” before the mission’s data is wired in.

Factors the team considered

  • Data honesty: keeping simulated and real data clearly separate.
  • Scientific limits: soil moisture, roughness, viewing geometry, speckle and season can all mimic real change.
  • Accessibility: plain language, a glossary and a radar-versus-optical comparison.
  • Responsible use: no emergency claims, and users are directed to official flood authorities.
  • Scalability: a design that can switch from simulated scenes to real NISAR products.
